target_customer: Authors, editors, designers and marketers who form a revenue-sharing publishing team per book, and book buyers
problem: Authors faced either gatekeeping by traditional publishers or doing everything themselves in self-publishing; Booktrope offered a team model with no upfront fees.
business_model: Hybrid publisher: kept about 30 percent of net profits, the rest split among the book team

founders.name: Kenneth Shear
previous_startups: Libertary (2009 website posting books free online, precursor of Booktrope)
founders.background_notes: Seattle magazine (Dec 2012) says he started a law office, helped launch information retrieval businesses and wrote a book on the First Amendment. Education not found.

founders.name: Andy Roberts
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as Founder/CTO with product management and software background.

founders.name: Katherine Sears
founders.background_notes: Internet marketing specialist who joined Shear after a Craigslist ad in 2010 per Seattle magazine.

exit.reason: Company cited a revenue shortfall; Publishers Weekly said the business model was no longer financially viable.

competitors.name: Amazon (publishing and Kindle self-publishing)
competitors.what: Seattle e-book publisher and self-publishing channel; Booktrope also distributed through Amazon

competitors.name: Traditional Big Six publishers
competitors.what: Gatekept submissions and paid low royalties per the article

competitors.name: Vanity presses and self-publishing
competitors.what: Authors paid for printing or hired their own editors and designers

technical_complexity.rationale: A team and royalty management platform with print and e-book distribution through existing channels; standard web engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Authors could leave and take their rights back, and the model could be copied; the main asset was a community of creatives.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying the model. The company shut down in May 2016 citing revenue shortfall.

market_need_then: Authors complained of low royalties and gatekeeping, and self-publishing was costly in time and skill. Booktrope published almost 1,000 titles and engaged about 1,100 creatives by its end per its CMO's YC bio.

branding.community_and_virality: Authors wrote public blog posts about the closure, showing an engaged author community.

brand_strength.rationale: Brand was known among indie authors and in publishing press (Jane Friedman, Publishers Weekly), but no evidence it was a growth driver. Precursor site was called Libertary, and a 2012 profile suggests that name drew objections; why the name became Booktrope is not stated.

outcome_analysis: Booktrope raised angel money in 2013 and about $1.2 million in a 2015 seed tied to YC, and published almost 1,000 titles, but its 30 percent share of net profits did not produce enough revenue. It announced closure in April 2016 and shut down at the end of May 2016. Publishers Weekly said changes in the book market made the model unviable, and that authors reclaiming rights may have hurt. The sources support a revenue and unit economics failure rather than a funding gap.
notes: The $1.2M seed (of a planned $2.3M per an SEC filing) and the $205K angel award come from search result summaries of GeekWire and Seattle Angel Conference pages; GeekWire pages returned 403 when fetched. A data aggregator lists $1.2M total over one round while Seedtable lists none. Angel award is labelled other because sources do not state a stage. Competitors cite a December 2012 profile, about two years before the W15 batch; Owler listed Inkshares, Unbound and Publishizer but that list is undated and was not used. The 11 employees figure and shutdown date of 2016-05-31 come from search summaries. booktrope.com redirects to a for-sale page.
